Gibbethon
GIB-eh-thon
proper noun
Hebrew Gibbethon, “a height” or “a mound,” a Philistine town in the lot of Dan, given to the Levites.

📖 Biblical Definition

Gibbethon was a town on the Philistine border, assigned to the tribe of Dan and given to the Levites of the Kohathite family (Josh 19:44; 21:23), but held by the Philistines through much of Israel’s history. Its siege became the scene of two royal assassinations in the northern kingdom. While Nadab the son of Jeroboam, with all Israel, laid siege to Gibbethon, Baasha conspired against him and slew him there, then reigned in his stead and destroyed all the house of Jeroboam (1Ki 15:27). A generation later, Israel was again encamped against Gibbethon when word came that Zimri had murdered Elah the son of Baasha; the army in the field made Omri their captain king, and he went up from Gibbethon to besiege Zimri in Tirzah (1Ki 16:15–17). Thus the same Philistine stronghold witnessed the fall of two dynasties of Israel, the houses of Jeroboam and of Baasha alike cut off in fulfillment of the word of the LORD. Gibbethon, a town Israel could never firmly hold, became instead the ground where the LORD’s judgments upon the apostate northern kings were set in motion. It is a sober monument to the truth that thrones built upon idolatry and bloodshed do not stand.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Philistine-held Levitical town in Dan, twice besieged by Israel; scene of the falls of the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha.

expand to see more

GIBBETHON, a town on the Philistine border in the lot of Dan.

It was assigned to the Levites of the Kohathites (Josh 21:23).

There Baasha slew Nadab while Israel besieged the town (1Ki 15:27).

There Israel made Omri king on hearing of Zimri’s treason (1Ki 16:16).

It remained long in the hands of the Philistines.

📖 Key Scripture

1Ki 15:27 — "And Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; and Baasha smote him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines; for Nadab and all Israel laid siege to Gibbethon."

1Ki 16:15 — "In the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah did Zimri reign seven days in Tirzah. And the people were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines."

1Ki 16:17 — "And Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah."

Josh 21:23 — "And out of the tribe of Dan, Eltekeh with her suburbs, Gibbethon with her suburbs,"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that thrones built on idolatry and blood do not stand.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s faithfulness to His threatenings. He had decreed the cutting off of Jeroboam’s house for its idolatry, and of Baasha’s house after it; and at Gibbethon, far from the throne-city, His word came to pass. The judgments of God upon sin are not idle words; they ripen in their season and fall with certainty.

Gibbethon also displays the unrest of the northern kingdom, where king murdered king and dynasty devoured dynasty. A kingdom founded in rebellion against the house of David and in the worship of golden calves knew no settled peace. Sin breeds disorder; the throne that despises God’s appointed order reaps treason and bloodshed in its own house.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name means “a height” or “mound,” fitting a town set upon raised ground near the Philistine plain.

expand to see more

Gibbethon — Hebrew Gibbethon, “a height” or “a mound.”

It lay in the lot of Dan toward the Philistine border.

It was given to the Kohathite Levites.

Twice Israel besieged it and twice a king fell during the siege.

The Philistine height became the ground of Israel’s dynastic ruin.

Usage

"Like the kings who fell at Gibbethon, thrones founded on idolatry and blood do not stand."

"Gibbethon teaches that the LORD’s threatenings against sin ripen and fall with certainty."

"The unrest at Gibbethon shows that a kingdom built in rebellion knows no settled peace."
